title: Thoughts on zazen from Zoketsu Norman Fischer
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads the first third of the meditation chapter in Zoketsu Norman Fischer's book The World Could Be Otherwise, part of Nomon's study of the six paramitas, and adds comments of Nomon's own. Norman traces the word meditation from Old French and Latin, describes the tripod of ethical conduct, meditation and understanding, and defines shamatha through Buddhaghosa's Visuddhimagga. Nomon lingers on the five hindrances: attachment, aversion, flurry and worry, laziness, and doubt. Norman's favorite practice is breathing in the lower belly, and he also offers the phrase "May all beings be happy." Nomon closes by sending everyone into groups of three to share what hindrances showed up in that evening's sitting.

It's been just such a great thing for us to have this period that feels a little more dialed up.

So that's making it to the website now.
It should be there in a couple of days, so you can see what's coming up.
And the regular schedule looks like it can roll right through the holidays, since most people aren't going anywhere.
We'll still have Wednesday evening and Monday through Thursday morning and Saturday morning, and starting in January, Sunday morning.
So if you want to do Zoom-based Zen, we've got you covered.
For the talk, I want to share a piece by Norman Fischer, at least part of a piece.
I've been really enjoying his book on the six paramitas, the six perfect practices of the bodhisattvas.
Our senior students gave talks on that last July if you were around.
This is what his book looks like.
It's called The World Could Be Otherwise, Norman Fischer.
It's all been pretty good, but I'm really super impressed with the meditation chapter.
I had already been thinking that now that we're taking a little pause from koan studies, it'd be good to really focus on zazen.
That's the main thing we do together.
So maybe we should talk a little bit about meditation, about zazen.
I was looking for different sources in my own experience, and of course Dogen has quite a few things to say about zazen.
He's a big fan.
But I thought we'd start with Norman.
Excuse me, I think I need a little more light to read this text.
So I'll just turn the light switch up.
I'm going to read about a third of this chapter on meditation and make a few comments of my own.
Then hopefully we can have some discussion, because what are we doing?
Or what are we not doing?
What's going on?
Is that half hour worth anything?
Or is it great because it's not worth anything?
Here's what Norman says.
*The word meditation is an English word from Old French and Latin, meaning to think over, to think deeply, to reflect.
And as such, meditation is not new to us in the West.
We have a long tradition of meditation as a form of thinking.
Of course, we're thinking all the time, mostly in scattered and unconscious ways.
To meditate is to think calmly, deeply, with focus and a serious intention.
Philosophical thought is meditative.
It requires that we step back from ordinary thinking, emotion driven planning and strategizing, to a profound consideration of what we most deeply value and understand.
But meditation is also a religious word.
It includes various practices Christian monastics and other Western religious practitioners have developed over the centuries.*
*We might more commonly call these practices contemplative.
Quiet, directed thinking inspired by faith and a sense of wonder or surrender.
Scripture, reading, prayer and sacred singing are, in this sense, forms of meditation.
Such meditation practices are also included within the range of Buddhist meditation.
But Indian meditation practice, Buddhist and pre-Buddhist, includes, in addition, a particular technique that our culture seems to lack.
The specific practice that we usually think of these days when we use the word meditation.
I'm talking about the psychophysical practice of concentration in which the meditator sits upright in a yogic posture on a meditation cushion or a chair, focused on breathing, silent and aware.*
*This powerful and simple practice is Indian culture's great gift to the world.
So radically simple.
Yet, as far as we know, no Western person ever thought of doing such a thing.*
I'll make an argument for hunters, maybe, in that kind of stillness.
In the next section, that's interesting, the word meditation.
The next section is called tripod.
*There are several words for meditation in classical Buddhism.
Bhavana, often translated as meditation, literally means cultivation, an agricultural word.
Cultivation implies discipline, careful, steady effort over time.
In other words, samadhi means concentration, focus, single-pointedness, non-distraction.
The word samadhi describes a state of mind rather than a technique or a practice, the result of disciplined meditation rather than an exercise.
Jhana is the word used for the fifth perfection.* Remember, this is the fifth of six perfect practices.
This is Jhana Paramita.
*Jhana refers to the practice of settling and focusing the mind.
Classical descriptions liken the Buddhist path to a tripod, where the three legs stand for the three great practices of ethical conduct, meditation and understanding.*
*As with a tripod, these legs must be in perfect balance.
These three practices evenly support one another and enable the path of practice, ethical conduct, meditation and understanding.
We could say that ethical conduct is the most important of the three, because the point of spiritual practice is to live truly and beautifully.
To support ethical conduct, we have to practice meditation to stabilize our ordinary shifting mind and heart.
When the mind is stable and the conduct pure, deep understanding will arise.
Understanding that is more than thinking and wishing, that suffuses our identity and our feeling for life.
With that suffusion, our behavior will naturally be forthright.
Or we could look at it like this instead.*
*Understanding is the point of spiritual practice.
In order to gain it, we have to start with ethical conduct, so we can reduce our problems and dramas.
And meditation is a necessity for the kind of deep understanding we're aiming for.
Understanding that pierces the veil of ordinary reality, ordinary confused thinking.
Or we could put meditation in the center of the path.
The point of spiritual practice is to live a focused and meditative life beyond the confusion of the everyday.
When meditation is our daily practice and approach to life, pure conduct and understanding will naturally arise.*
You see how I did that?
That was really clever, huh?
It could be this, it could be this one, it could be this one.
So it must be all three.
*And however we look at it, whichever we think comes first or last or is the most or least important, it's clear that the tripod needs all three legs.
They always go together.
It's as if they are one and the same.
According to traditional descriptions, the specific function of meditation is to deepen and stabilize the mind and heart.
Deepen and stabilize the mind and heart.
Stabilization and depth are necessary if conduct and understanding are to be firm and serious.
If they are to touch us to the point that we experience transformation.
Without meditation, our best intentions just wobble.
We find ourselves frequently locked off our game by events and our reactions to them.
We undergo all sorts of waffling which erodes our good conduct and calm understanding.
Since meditation involves somatic as well as psychological cultivation,* somatic is the body, *it affects us at a deeper level than ordinary thinking and feeling.
It touches us all the way down to the breath and the body, down to our bones, the seat of our feeling, thinking and emotion, our body.*
Next section is called shamatha, calming or concentrating meditation.
I just want to read this section.
*Classically, Buddhist meditation is divided into two major branches of practice, two practices.
Shamatha or calming meditation and vipassana or insight meditation.
In some presentations of meditation, shamatha is developed first as a basis for vipassana.
In others, the two are developed simultaneously or in tandem.
Sometimes the two are collapsed into one practice with two aspects.*
So calming and insight, two big branches.
*In Buddhagosa's classic text, the 5th century Vesuddha Magga, path of purification, shamatha is understood as concentration.
Buddhagosa begins by asking the question, what is concentration?
Many answers that concentration is of so many types and aspects, it would be impossible to discuss them all.
He further argues that such a discussion would lead to distraction anyway, the opposite of concentration.
So he concludes by provisionally defining concentration as profitable unification of the mind.
Profitable, beneficial unification of the mind.
Unification in the sense of being without distraction or division, a mind anchored to one point.
Profitable in the sense of spiritually profitable, tending towards understanding, liberation and compassion.* So compassion is unification of the mind in the service of spiritual growth.
Concentration, I said the wrong word.
So concentration is unification of the mind, in the course of spiritual growth, so not so divided up.
*Buddhagosa's thorough discussion of concentration includes many hundreds of pages of practices, most of which have probably not been used for centuries.

But his list also includes practices that are used today, such as concentration on the body, concentration on breathing, concentration on the four unlimited emotions of loving-kindness, sympathetic joy, compassion and equanimity.
The basic technique for concentration involves bringing the mind to the object of concentration and patiently training it through repetition to stay on that object, and this is not easy to do.
The mind gets distracted, tired and or bored.
It's not used to staying put unless it has some distinct drive towards pleasure or satisfaction, or avoiding the opposite,* right?
*But when you try to concentrate in meditation, you are impressed with how little control you actually have over your mind.
It's humbling to realize that you can tell your mind in all seriousness, stay still, but it won't stay still.
You can't control it.
It makes you wonder who is in charge of whom.
Still, if you keep at it, you eventually develop some ability to focus.
Maybe once in a while you come into a moment of strong, single-pointed concentration, which is peaceful and calming.
Developing concentration takes much more time than you might have thought.* We know that.
*It takes faith, diligence, determination and support.
Traditional texts define five hindrances to meditation that anyone who tries to meditate will sooner or later see.
Five are attachment, the mind's obsession with thoughts, memories, sensations or images other than the meditation object.* So first is attachment, desire for something.
*Aversion, obsessively complaining and the desire to flee and get rid of things.* Third one, he translates as flurry and worry.
Flurry and worry.
*Distractedness, really.
The mind and body jumping all over the place and dredging up things to be concerned about, doing anything not to stay with the object of concentration.
Fourth of five is laziness, being sleepy and unmotivated and thus unable to return to the object for lack of interest.
Doubt.
Wondering what is the point of doing all this frustrating and boring work anyway or doubting one's capability to even do it.
When one of these five hindrances and their various related mental and emotional states is present, concentration just can't be.* It's interesting.
Concentration can't be if a hindrance is present.
*So the practice of concentration involves identifying them and patiently working through them until they reduce and eventually disappear.
Although they will reappear.
Of course these five hindrances can occur anytime.
Not only in meditation.
So the ability to stay focused and not let them get the best of you has implications for your life beyond the development of meditation.
When you're able to get beyond the hindrances or at least temporarily understand them in meditation, then concentration states spontaneously appear.
Bringing emotional and physical delight, joy and equanimity.
All of which can feel quite wonderful.
While calm this meditation, this shamatha meditation, may be a struggle, its rewards are unexpectedly great.
Most experienced meditators who have some capacity to concentrate enjoy their practice.
Would rather meditate than spend their time in many other pursuits.*
*Breathing is probably the most common and effective concentration object.
There are many ways to do breathing meditation practice.
My favorite is to pay attention to breathing in the lower belly.
Watching the breath as it rises and falls, rises and falls there.
And feeling the sensation of breathing infusing the whole body.
Infusing the whole body.
Breathing consciously is a pleasure.
It is calming, healthy, has good effects on your mood, outlook, and capacity to think straight even in trying situations.
If you can keep focus on the breath in meditation, you'll eventually feel a deep sense of life's rhythm in and out.
In and out, coming and going, again and again, peacefully.
You can feel as if you're breathing with everything and everyone on the planet.
And that breathing is breathing you into existence.
Breathing is breathing you into existence.
And constantly takes care of everything, leaving you with nothing to worry about.
The same kind of focus practice can be done using a feeling, a word, or a phrase as the object instead of the breath.
Many practitioners now and in the past have meditated on loving kindness or other social emotions.
Produce the same sort of focus meditation states.*
*Here the technique is to bring the mind again and again back to a phrase, such as, may all beings be happy.* Helps to feel connected to beings too.
*May all beings be happy.
And the feeling that goes with it.
Perhaps try situating the phrase in the belly and repeat it with the breath.
With this practice, the feeling of concentration becomes infused with a heartfelt goodwill for others.
May all beings be happy.
Practices such as these make it clear that concentration meditation is more than technical exercise for producing mental focus.
A skillful bank robber or assassin can develop strong mental focus with concentration techniques too.
Meditative concentration is, as Buddhaghosa says, humane, ethical.
Connecting us to others and liberating us from the self-focus and distraction.
Liberating us from the self-focus and distraction that make our lives small and unimaginative.
The paradox of calming meditation practice is that while it does narrow your mind to a single point, that point is expansive.
A window, so to speak, onto vast vistas beyond.*

I thought we'd pause there and have some discussion.
It's been a while since we've used the small group feature, where it's so much easier to talk, but also one may feel a little on the spot.
So just remember you can always pass or just say something really simple.
Nobody has to be brilliant here.

So let's just reflect on what we heard.
We haven't heard yet the payoff about what this calming meditation is as opposed to the insight meditation, so probably don't worry about that too much.
But think about the actual enterprise of stabilizing the mind, this calming meditation, which is very much a part of zazen that we were just doing.

You might talk about whether you noticed any of the five hindrances: being attached to something being otherwise, being averse to something that's happening, being flurried and worried, distracted, right?
I'm blanking on the fourth one right now because I'm a little flurried and worried too, I guess.
Oh yeah, laziness, sleepiness, drowsiness.
Just checking out a little bit.
And just doubting the whole thing.

Remember what he said, they're natural.
They always will arise.
You can work with them so they arise less, but then even a very experienced practitioner, writing this book, said they'll reappear anyway, so don't worry about it too much.
So just be curious in your small group discussion: were any of those hindrances present?
You could use your own words for them.
And the last thing he was talking about is the how of it.
In a way, we're not trying to do a darn thing, right?
We're trying to do less, to not disturb the mind, to let things settle.
But we seem to need a direction or a place to point our effort.
So he talked about breath meditation, feeling the breath in the belly being a favorite, and that's one of our favorites here too.
We also sometimes like to support the breath awareness with counting practice.
But he also mentioned working with phrases, and a few of you are working with different phrases.
And he mentioned loving kindness.
So there is some creativity and some flexibility to this enterprise.
You just talk about what you are doing, what hindrances are popping up, and what happened tonight.
Not in general, because that's turning this into a story of a story.
It's already a story because the last meditation period is long gone, but maybe you can remember something of what actually happened as an experience.
Just share a little bit.
If your thoughts take you other places, like how meditation does or doesn't work in the rest of your life, that's wonderful.
This idea that he had in here, that stability of mind is not just a meditative trick, or it's not just becoming a meditation athlete.
How do you think this kind of stability has benefited you in your life?
And also, have you noticed times lately when you've had the opposite experience, right?
The mind very topsy-turvy, flurried and worried and resistant.
What does that do?
Because in the end, we're working with our body and mind in a certain way.
We're simplifying things down and taking a certain stance, but it's a stance that we hope will really infuse our whole life.
So not to be like I'm a meditator or I do meditation in the morning or something like that, but life as meditation, right?
A meditative life, a contemplative life.
So let's spend about ten minutes on that.
I'm shooting for groups of three.
If you're on the same screen, then we'll just see what happens, with somebody else, I mean to say.
Hold on, I've got to mess around a little bit with the arrangements.
Okay, that looks like groups of three.
Okay, see you in ten.
Have a good conversation.
